brief.analysis: The bet is that aerospace and defense falls back versus the S&P 500, but the flat-average and trend-adjusted readings of this relationship disagree by more than a full step, which is direct evidence the 'normal' level is drifting upward rather than sitting still. That drift lines up with a structural spending shift: NATO members have pledged to raise defense budgets toward 5% of GDP from 2%, a durable tailwind, and none of the moving-average checks confirm a turn (0 of 3). The move back to the one-year average is essentially already done (+0.1%), and the further 18% to the five-year average targets a mean that has almost certainly moved higher.
brief.report_line: Avoid shorting defense-versus-S&P: the relationship's baseline is drifting up on the NATO 2%-to-5%-of-GDP spending shift, the trend-adjusted reading contradicts the flat average, and momentum offers no confirmation of a turn.

brief.analysis: Silver ran violently ahead of gold and has already snapped most of the way back, with the trade's one-year-average target now achieved, so the easy money is largely made. The problem is that both legs are being reshaped structurally: silver is in its fifth straight year of supply deficit with record industrial demand from solar, EVs and AI, while gold is bid by record central-bank buying, so neither metal is simply mean-reverting. The remaining pull toward the five-year average (about +13%) rests on an average that both regime shifts have probably moved, so take what reversion is left but do not lean on the old mean.
brief.report_line: Short silver-versus-gold has already delivered most of its snap-back; hold small for residual reversion but the five-year average target is suspect given silver's supply deficits and record central-bank gold demand.

brief.analysis: The bet is that chipmakers give back ground against the broad Nasdaq, and a recent pullback (the chip basket already fell about 9.5% in a month) gives the snap-back a running start. But the AI build-out is a genuine multi-year spending wave, not a blip: the big cloud buyers are guiding 2026 capital budgets above $400 billion versus roughly $230 billion in 2024, which can keep chips permanently richer than history. The engine only asks for the modest move back to the roughly one-year average (about +10%), which is realistic; the full 61% move to the five-year average is not a valid target and should not be traded.
brief.report_line: Short chips-versus-Nasdaq for the tactical move back toward its one-year average only, sized down, because the AI capex boom means the old five-year relationship may never return.
